title: Prefix, Suffix, Greedy
focus: Two sweeps instead of division, versioned storage, and the day greedy beats DP.

cards.title: Prefix and Suffix Sweeps
cards.trigger: Every element needs an aggregate of everything except itself.
cards.recall: Write product-except-self from memory in O(1) extra space. Then answer: what does the output array hold after the first pass, and how does the running suffix variable finish the job?
useWhen: Product or sum of the array except self, without division
Candy distribution, two passes for two constraints
Trapping rain water, the two-array version
Best time to buy and sell with a forward min and a backward max
Any 'for each i, use everything on both sides' question
template: # Pass 1: out[i] = product of everything strictly LEFT of i
# Pass 2: multiply in the product of everything strictly RIGHT of i
return out          # output array does not count as extra space
# left pass  : if rating[i] > rating[i-1], candy[i] = candy[i-1] + 1
# right pass : if rating[i] > rating[i+1], candy[i] = max(candy[i], candy[i+1] + 1)
keyInsights: Assign before you accumulate. Doing it the other way round includes the element itself
Division fails on zeros and is usually explicitly banned. Two sweeps sidestep both problems
The candy problem shows the general form: one sweep per direction of constraint, then combine with max
cards.trap: 'Does the output array count as extra space?' Standard answer: no, output is not counted. Say it rather than assuming they agree.

cards.title: Versioned Storage
patterns: Key to sorted list of versions
cards.trigger: Values change over time and you must retrieve the state as of a given moment.
cards.recall: Sketch the structure from memory and write `get`. Then answer why binary search is valid here without any explicit sorting step.
useWhen: Time-based key-value store, get the value at or before a timestamp
Snapshot arrays, get the value at a snapshot id
Version control style lookups
Interval or calendar bookings, find the applicable entry
Any 'as of time T' query
template: # first index with timestamp > target, then step back one
keyInsights: The list is sorted because the problem guarantees increasing timestamps. If it did not, you would need a sorted container
`bisect_right` then step back is the standard 'largest value at or below' idiom. Learn that pairing
The sentinel high character makes the tuple compare correctly regardless of the value stored
cards.trap: 'Timestamps can arrive out of order.' Append-and-binary-search breaks. You need insort, which is O(n) per set, or a balanced tree. State the trade.

cards.title: Mirror and Invert
cards.trigger: A question about a tree's reflection rather than its contents.
cards.recall: Write both invert and the symmetry check from memory. Then answer: symmetry compares `a.left` to `b.right`. Say why, and why comparing a tree to its own inversion is a worse solution.
useWhen: Symmetric tree, invert a binary tree
Check if two trees are mirrors
Boundary traversal, left boundary and reversed right boundary
Flip equivalent binary trees
Any reflection or mirror-image question
template: if not a and not b: return True
if not a or not b:  return False
return not root or mirror(root.left, root.right)
# Iterative symmetry: a queue holding PAIRS
keyInsights: The cross comparison, left against right, is the whole idea. Comparing left to left checks equality, not symmetry
Inverting then comparing mutates the input and doubles the work. Say why the direct check is better
The iterative form queues pairs rather than nodes, which generalises to any two-tree comparison
cards.trap: 'Flip equivalent: you may swap children at any node.' Now you compare both pairings at each node and recurse into whichever matches. Strictly harder than symmetry.

cards.title: Greedy over DP
cards.trigger: A DP is available, and a single sweep with one running maximum is provably just as good.
cards.recall: Write jump game II from memory in O(n). Then answer the question they will ask: why is greedy correct here, and what is the argument that you never miss a better choice?
useWhen: Jump game, minimum jumps, can you reach the end
Gas station circuit
Assign cookies, task assignment by sorted matching
Partition labels, extend the boundary as you sweep
Any DP where the optimal choice is provably local
template: # Minimum jumps: each 'level' is one jump. This is BFS without a queue.
for i in range(len(nums) - 1):        # stop before the last index
if i == current_end:              # exhausted this jump's range
# Can you reach the end at all?
# Partition labels: extend the current chunk to the last index of every char in it
last = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(s)}
keyInsights: `current_end` is the boundary of what the current jump count can reach. Crossing it means you spent another jump. That is BFS by levels
Looping to n-2 is deliberate. Standing on the last index means you have arrived and must not count another jump
Greedy needs an argument, not a vibe. Here: taking the furthest reach can never be worse, because reachability is a prefix
cards.trap: 'Prove your greedy is optimal.' If you cannot give the exchange argument in two sentences, write the O(n^2) DP instead and say you would prove it before shipping.

cards.title: Constraint Backtracking
cards.trigger: Place items under mutual-exclusion constraints, and you must find all valid placements.
cards.recall: Write N-Queens from memory. Then answer the encoding question that makes it fast: how do you identify the two diagonals of a cell with two integers?
useWhen: N-Queens, N-Queens II
Sudoku solver, three constraint sets per digit
Graph colouring on a small graph
Any exact-cover style placement
Crossword or tiling fill under constraints
template: cols, diag, anti = set(), set(), set()
if c in cols or (row - c) in diag or (row + c) in anti:
# row - c is constant along a '\' diagonal
# row + c is constant along a '/' diagonal
keyInsights: One queen per row is assumed by the structure, so rows never need checking. That single decision removes a whole constraint
`row - c` and `row + c` are constant along the two diagonals, which turns an O(n) scan into an O(1) set lookup
Un-choosing must undo all three sets. Forgetting one produces missing solutions rather than a crash, which is much harder to debug
cards.trap: 'Just count the solutions, do not list them.' Now you can use bitmasks instead of sets and it runs an order of magnitude faster. Know the bitmask version exists.
